A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same event-based tracking framework, renamed MATE in v2. The text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. All supplied material was inspected, including v2's supplementary Sections 6–9; v1 contains no separate supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original tracking experiments on Ev-PointOdyssey, EC and EDS, component ablations, and qualitative analyses in Tables 1–3 and Figures 5–8.

after.justification: v2 reports original tracking results across four datasets, revised component ablations, and supplementary representation and hyperparameter experiments in Table 4 and Figure 9.

M1.justification: The stated supervision changes from MAE in v1 to temporally weighted absolute error with gamma=0.8 in v2 Equation 8. The central MGM and VMAM/VMA architecture remains. Expanded descriptions of feature pyramids, encoder blocks and two temporal convolutions do not independently establish architectural changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds Ev-Davis, simulated from TAP-Vid-Davis real videos, extending TAP evaluation to scenes with fast motion and frequent occlusion. Ev-PointOdyssey, EC and EDS remain. Feature tracking itself is retained coverage, despite receiving a separate task subsection.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains PIPs++ but removes PIPs, TAPIR, Context-PIPs, EKLT, DeepEvT, E-RAFT and B-FLOW from that comparison, adding CoTracker, CoTracker3 and event-adapted PIPs++/CoTracker3. Table 2 retains EKLT and DeepEvT while adding PIPs++, CoTracker3, FE-TAP, EM-ICP, HASTE, AEB-Tracker and ETAP.

E3.justification: v1 describes 256×320 training followed by 512×640 fine-tuning; v2 reports training at 512×640. v2 introduces event-retrained video trackers as comparison controls, Survival16 evaluation for Ev-Davis, and supplementary experiments at 192×256 without VMA. FPS evaluation is removed. These are changes to reported protocols, not proof of which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The component-ablation design is retained, while supplementary Table 4 and Figure 9 add event-representation comparisons and sensitivity analyses for loss weighting and iteration count. Figure 7 replaces the MLP kinematic-vector correction visualization with an MGM-on/off tracking case. Occlusion and rapid-motion case studies are also revised and expanded.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Figure 8 retains temporal standard deviations of feature activations; these are a feature-consistency analysis, not uncertainty estimates across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 contain substantially revised results. Ours' Ev-PointOdyssey accuracy/Survival50 changes from 0.358/0.553 to 0.362/0.560, and EDS FA/EFA from 0.616/0.529 to 0.713/0.626. Ev-Davis and supplementary results are added; FPS results are removed. Changed training descriptions and MTE scaling prevent interpreting these as unqualified same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit mathematical definition of temporally weighted supervision in Equation 8, including the gamma-based weighting absent from v1's MAE description. The surface-gradient, plane-fitting and event-rate derivations otherwise remain, with renumbering and notation changes rather than new proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions remove the 150% faster-processing claim and instead emphasize a 17.9% Survival50 advantage over an event-only TAP baseline and superiority to feature trackers using events plus frames. The dataset contribution expands from one simulated event dataset to two. The central motion-guidance and temporal-consistency claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for sampling offset-frame features, time-surface advantages over other representations, and the accuracy/computation tradeoff around six iterations. It also explains why missing ground truth for occluded Ev-Davis points limits visualization. The main interpretation based on motion guidance and temporal consistency is retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents encoder structure, polarity-separated time surfaces, sampling strides, approximately 340k training samples with 128 points each, augmentations, and spline alignment of feature-tracking ground truth. Reported hardware changes from four to eight A6000 GPUs. Conversely, v1's event-simulation/interpolation recipe and project-page link disappear. Newly disclosed implementation details do not establish that those procedures changed.

R1.justification: v1 states that event-based TAP has not yet been proposed. v2 discusses FE-TAP and ETAP and positions MATE against their appearance-based matching, materially revising its novelty framing. Additional tracker references support the expanded comparisons, while the simulator and frame-interpolation references are removed.

P1.justification: The method overview and module explanations are substantially rewritten. Experiments are reorganized from combined quantitative/qualitative comparisons into implementation details, TAP, feature tracking and ablations. The paper is retitled MATE, VMAM becomes VMA, and dedicated supplementary sections are introduced.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is extensively redrawn, Table 1 gains a second dataset and loses FPS, and Table 2 gains modality groups and numerous comparator rows. Figures 4–7 replace or expand visual examples; supplementary Table 4 and Figures 9–11 are added. Figure 8 largely retains its existing analysis.

improvement.justification: Ev-Davis and event-adapted TAP comparisons substantially strengthen the evidence for generalization and comparative performance. Targeted ablations and the implementation supplement also address important gaps in assessing and reproducing v1. These gains outweigh the loss of FPS results, simulation instructions and the project link. Claims still need qualification: v2 says it outperforms all feature trackers, but Table 2 reports EC EFA of 0.875 versus ETAP's 0.876.
